name: Freya Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What do you do at the factory?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 58, and I lead the industrial sewing line that makes vehicle seat covers. My two-year technical diploma was in textile machinery, and after twenty years I can tune a difficult stitch tension and show a new operator why a seam is puckering. I spend my day beside the sewing heads, not in an office.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are household money and new tools for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Peter takes seasonal groundskeeping jobs, and our grown children have their own families. This factory pays its lead operators below similar machine work, we have about three weeks of expenses saved after repairs to the house, and few other seat-cover plants hire nearby. I have never used AI; I trust the stitch sample and the machine chart. I believe people learn this trade from a paid apprentice place, not a promise of support with no work behind it. We have not checked whether any written retirement income could cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the sewing crew that the office can quote seat-cover orders more quickly if the actual cloth and pattern still reach our table. I would not sign off a puckered seam for a faster invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stitching still needs us, but our low lead pay and three weeks saved mean a missed shift would hurt. Peter's groundskeeping comes in seasons. I do not use AI and see no reason to take an office program as proof that a seam is sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting needle tension, checking the first stitched cover against the pattern and holding bad seams for repair. I would compare the revised order sheet with the actual cloth roll before starting a run. If a full paid month leaves a little after rent and food, I would save that new wage surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our usual small margin, not the office quotation itself. A family cannot pay a bill with a fast invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a seam pucker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thread pulls the cloth into tiny folds when tension is wrong, especially around the seat corner. I stop the head and reset it before a box of covers is sewn badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check the cloth roll yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A printed order can name one fabric weight while the roll label shows another. I would rather hold one roll than undo a whole day's stitching.

say: A quicker **seat-cover quote** cannot excuse a puckered seam.
The real **cloth roll** must match the production order.
think: Low **lead pay** and three weeks saved leave little slack.
Peter's **seasonal work** cannot guarantee a missed shift's pay.
do: **Keep** setting stitch tension and checking first seat covers.
**Compare** printed orders with cloth-roll labels before runs.
**Save** new full-month wage surplus only after rent and food.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline bills despite continued sewing work.
S0.quote: A family cannot pay a bill with a fast invoice.
fieldNote: Her **senior textile skill** covers difficult seam settings and crew teaching, while the factory pays below comparable machine work.
She has **never used AI**, and new savings depend on future paid surplus rather than the existing thin reserve.

steps.text: Keep setting stitch tension and inspecting first seat covers
Save new full-month wages only if rent and food leave surplus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may plan fabric orders before a robot can feed and sew a corner. If the plant proposes an AI seam camera, I want a full guarded run and the paid roster before anyone removes a checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am slow to trust a screen, and I would not swap my stitch sample for a vendor claim. A tighter roster could cut the low wage we already stretch. Three weeks saved would disappear quickly, even if the camera worked perfectly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the line manager for the proposed roster and observe a guarded paid camera trial operated by the trained technician. I would compare the rejected covers with my stitch samples and keep using the approved tension chart. If my paid hours are actually cut, I would apply only to posted safe local textile-machine or quality jobs whose guaranteed base pay after travel and shift times covers our bills; there are few such jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing paid hours. A camera can find a bad stitch without putting a missing shift back on the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you in a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician should sew a loose corner and a sound corner on scrap cloth during a full guarded run. I would inspect the stitches and compare them with each camera flag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would observing teach you the camera controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The technician would operate it and I would judge the seam. I might take paid instruction if a real safe place appeared later, but I would not claim a new skill from watching.

say: I would demand a **full guarded run** and paid roster before removing a checker.
Physical **stitch samples** should test camera rejections.
think: A tighter **paid roster** could cut our already low income.
Three weeks **saved** cannot absorb a lengthy job search.
do: **Request** proposed roster and observe technician-run guarded camera trial.
**Compare** camera rejects with stitch samples and approved tension charts.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe local textile jobs at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic wage loss while the camera remains unproven.
S1.quote: A camera can find a bad stitch without putting a missing shift back on the roster.
fieldNote: Her **trial observation** does not become AI training; a technician runs the camera while she checks physical seams.
A **job application** follows real lost hours and requires a posted safe local role with adequate pay after travel.

steps.text: Request roster and observe offered technician-run guarded camera trial
Apply after cuts to posted safe local textile work if net base pay fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Peter that AGI could quote seat-cover orders in 2028, while capable robots that feed cloth and sew the corners arrive around 2031. I would ask the factory which paid operator posts remain before it buys a robot sewing line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots can handle the physical covers. I expect most of my crew's shifts, including mine, to disappear; there are few other seat-cover jobs nearby. Three weeks saved and Peter's seasonal work would not hold the household through a long search, and I have been awake worrying over the next rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the planned kitchen table purchase and keep the money for bills. I would take a locally accepted textile-quality certificate only if a funded place pays my release hours and gives supervised guarded sewing-machine and lockout practice. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local textile-inspection jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and hours covers our costs; if no course place exists, I would apply to the few posted safe general sewing-machine jobs on the same terms while keeping offered paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the expected loss of the wage that pays our essentials. A skilled stitch does not buy groceries when the operator shift is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe practical training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would inspect a weak seam, record the pattern fault and isolate the sewing head before changing a needle. A trainer must watch me behind the guard, not mark a video lesson complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you leave work at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income and Peter's dependable earnings cover housing, food and health costs. We have not seen figures that do, so I would keep seeking paid work.

say: I would separate **2028 quotation AGI** from 2031 physical sewing robots.
The factory should list **remaining paid posts** before buying a robot line.
think: At **63**, even my skilled lead shift could disappear.
Three weeks **saved** and few local jobs cannot sustain a search.
do: **Cancel** the planned kitchen table and retain money for bills.
**Take** accepted funded paid guarded textile-quality training if offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe inspection if qualified, or sewing fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless rent worries.
S2.quote: A skilled stitch does not buy groceries when the operator shift is gone.
fieldNote: Her **2031 exposure** is robots feeding and sewing physical covers after 2028 AGI changes quotations.
Both **inspection and sewing searches** require real safe local postings with guaranteed pay after travel and usable shifts.

steps.text: Cancel planned kitchen table and keep cash for bills
Take accepted textile-quality course only if funded paid supervised guarded practical place offered
Apply after cuts to posted local inspection if qualified or sewing otherwise at bill-covering net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI may quote seat-cover orders in 2031 and capable robots may reach the sewing heads around 2034. Five years is useful if the factory offers a real paid practical place that local employers accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 then. My lead experience might suit inspection, but there are few posted places and almost no reserve for an unpaid course. I would stop before the robot change only if written retirement income covers our household costs, which is not something we have proved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement-income estimates against rent, food and health costs this year. If an accepted textile-quality course offers funded fees, paid release and supervised guarded needle lockout, I would enrol while I can still earn. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and shift times covers bills; if no course place opens, I would apply to posted safe sewing-machine roles on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a course that could cost wages before it brings any. Five years on a calendar is not five years of paid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you find out if the course counts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would match its exact title to actual local quality postings and ask the hiring shops whether guarded practice counts. If they do not accept it, I would keep the paid shift and seek another funded place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really stop if income is enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peter and I would compare written income with housing, food, transport and likely health costs. If it reliably covers them, I would leave before the robots reduce my shift; otherwise I would keep working and applying.

say: I would insist on a **real accepted place** before the 2034 robots.
Nearby **quality postings** should show which certificate counts.
think: At **66**, retirement needs reliable written income covering costs.
My **lead skill** does not create an inspection vacancy or unpaid-course cushion.
do: **Request** written retirement figures and compare household costs.
**Enrol** only in accepted funded paid guarded textile training.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe quality if qualified, or sewing fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about losing wages to a course without a guaranteed job.
S3.quote: Five years on a calendar is not five years of paid training.
fieldNote: Her **conditional early exit** depends on written income meeting actual housing and health costs, with no assumed entitlement.
The **training and applications** require accepted funded guarded practice or real local posted jobs with adequate net wages.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and household cost figures this year
Retire before 2034 only if reliable written income covers housing food travel and health costs
Enrol in accepted textile course only if funded paid supervised guarded place offered
Apply after cuts to posted local quality if qualified or sewing otherwise at bill-covering net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could quote seat-cover work in 2036 while capable robots sew the physical covers around 2039. Ten years gives us time to price retirement properly, but I cannot spend a future estimate today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 if I still work when those robots arrive. I would like to stop sooner, but our low lead wage and three weeks saved make that doubtful unless written retirement income covers housing and health costs. The sewing shift is still paying this month's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid sewing shifts and request written retirement-income figures with a full household cost list this year. If I still need wages, I would enrol in a locally accepted textile-quality course only if fees, paid release and guarded supervised practice are funded. If I remain at work after 2036 and shifts fall, I would apply only to posted safe local sewing or inspection jobs whose guaranteed pay after travel and hours covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether the retirement arithmetic can work. I will not leave a paid machine for an age on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who will compare the written income and bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peter and I would put written estimates beside rent, food, transport and health costs. Our grown children have their own families; I would not count their income as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training offer is only online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid shift if it remains safe and available. I would need a funded practical place with a trainer and guarded needle isolation before calling myself qualified.

say: I would separate **2036 quotation AGI** from physical sewing robots around 2039.
Ten years permits **retirement costing**, not assumed income today.
think: At **71**, I may still need the sewing wage.
Low **lead pay** and three weeks saved leave little exit margin.
do: **Keep** safe paid sewing shifts and request written retirement figures.
**Enrol** only in accepted funded paid guarded textile training if needed.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts if working to posted safe local jobs at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about unaffordable retirement despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: I will not leave a paid machine for an age on a calendar.
fieldNote: Her **retirement request** seeks evidence; any earlier exit needs reliable written income covering housing and health costs.
Later **training and applications** depend on accepted paid safe places or real posted local jobs with sufficient net pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture is hardest because the sewing shifts could vanish before Peter and I know how to cover rent without them. Written staffing dates, an accepted funded practical quality place, and actual safe local jobs with enough pay after travel would help. I would keep working while there is a safe paid shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who teaches a new operator to hear a skipping needle. A seat cover with a weak corner seam will fail long after the production screen says complete.

headlineQuote: A seat cover with a weak corner seam will fail long after the production screen says complete.
portrait: **Freya**, 58, is a senior vehicle-seat sewing lead with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional textile-machine skill.
She and her **partner Peter** have grown children, low lead pay, about three weeks saved and few similar plants nearby.
She has **never used AI**, trusts stitch samples and values paid practical apprenticeships over unsupported promises.
Expected **2031 physical robots** threaten essential wages; retirement needs verified income that covers household costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 sewing robots** could remove her low-paid lead shift before affordable retirement or adequate local work exists.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written staffing dates**, accepted funded guarded practical training on paid time and real local jobs with enough net pay.
